- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥ 0.5) over recent days, model tends to overestimate prices; reduce forecast slightly.
- If sentiment is negative (≤ 0.0) or near zero, model often underestimates; increase forecast to reflect risk aversion or market weakness.
- After a sharp price spike (forecast > 65.0), model frequently overcorrects downward; cap downward revisions at 5–10% of spike magnitude.
- Model underestimates mean-reverting trends in 30-day horizon; add 0.5–1.0% buffer to forecast if recent 7-day average is below 63.0.
- When sentiment history shows repeated small negative swings (e.g., 0.0–0.2), model tends to lag; adjust forecast up by 0.5–1.5 points for next period.
- If forecast is consistently 1–2 points below true outcome over 3–5 periods, model is underestimating volatility; increase forecast by 0.3–0.7 points per period.
- For 30-day forecasts, if sentiment is rising (e.g., 0.5–0.8), model often misses upward momentum; add 0.5–1.5 points to forecast if sentiment > 0.6.
- If forecast is > 68.0 and true outcome is < 66.0, model overestimates bullish sentiment; reduce forecast by 1–2 points if sentiment < 0.6.
